sentences.text: This dinosaur is defined by tall neural spines on its vertebrae that likely anchored a massive muscle ridge running from the neck to the hips.
It was a bipedal predator featuring a prominent hump over its back and hips supported by these high spines.
The animal possessed a skull measuring between 1.23 and 1.29 meters in length within a total body length of 11 to 12 meters.
Its upper jaw contained nineteen curved, serrated teeth on each side designed for processing prey.
The largest known specimen reached a length of 11 to 11.5 meters and weighed between 4.4 and 8.4 metric tons.
Fossil evidence indicates a powerful bite capable of generating an anterior force of 8,266 newtons and a posterior force of 16,894 newtons.
The holotype specimen displays a fractured and healed neural spine on the eleventh vertebra alongside an unusual hook-like structure on the third tail vertebra.
American paleontologists Stovall and Langston formally named and described the genus in 1950.
Definite fossils have been recovered from geological formations across Texas, Oklahoma, Wyoming, Arizona, Utah, and Maryland.
The forelimbs did not contact the ground and were utilized for hunting rather than for walking.
The arm could not reach a vertical position when swinging down but could swing up to 9 degrees above horizontal.
Like other non-avian theropods, the arms did not touch the ground and served hunting purposes instead of locomotion.
The shoulder joint had limited range of motion, allowing the arm to retract 109 degrees from the vertical but preventing a full circular movement.
Large olfactory bulbs suggest the animal possessed a keen sense of smell.
Reconstruction of the ear canal implies the head was held at a horizontal angle of less than 25 degrees when the animal was alert.
When accounting for lost Harris lines, the species likely required 18 to 24 years to reach maturity.
The brain structure was most similar to that of allosauroids rather than other theropod groups.
The brain resembles those of Carcharodontosaurus and Giganotosaurus, supporting the hypothesis that it was a carcharodontosaurid.
Brain reconstruction supports the hypothesis that Acrocanthosaurus was a carcharodontosaurid, showing similarities to Allosaurus and Sinraptor rather than other theropods.
The genus is classified within the superfamily Allosauroidea and the infraorder Tetanurae.
Most studies classify Acrocanthosaurus as a member of the family Carcharodontosauridae.
It is also classified within the family Carcharodontosauridae.
The animal lived during the Early Cretaceous Barremian and Late Cretaceous Cenomanian periods.
Fossils were found in an environment consisting of a large floodplain draining into a shallow inland sea.
Researchers suggest that differences between specimens may indicate a need to reexamine North American carcharodontosaurid material, potentially revealing greater diversity than previously thought.
It is debated whether the Glen Rose trackways represent a pack of Acrocanthosaurus stalking sauropods, as other explanations exist and the hypothesis is difficult to prove.
There is an ongoing debate regarding Acrocanthosaurus's evolutionary relationships, with some scientists classifying it as an allosaurid and others as a carcharodontosaurid.
